screens.title: NoSQL and DynamoDB data model
screens.narratorSegment: NoSQL databases use models other than fixed relational tables to store data. In DynamoDB you work with items and attributes rather than rows and columns; items in the same table can have different attributes. This schema-less flexibility is powerful when your application evolves quickly or when different entities share storage but need different fields. Concretely, a UserProfile table might contain items with fields like UserID, Email, Username, FullName and Age for some users, while others might include device tokens or preferences. DynamoDB supports both a simple key-value pattern and a richer document style where attributes can be nested. The core trade-off is flexibility versus relational guarantees: you gain agility and scale but accept that joins and complex multi-row transactions are not the primary pattern. A common misconception is that schema-less means you do not plan the shape of your data; in fact, you should design access patterns and keys up front to ensure efficient queries and even distribution. Example: a mobile backend storing profiles and optional settings benefits from adding only attributes you need per user. Takeaway: think in terms of access patterns and item-level attributes before choosing keys and indexes. What common queries will your application run against the data?

keyIdea.title: Schema-less, plan access patterns
keyIdea.text: DynamoDB stores flexible items; design around how you will query data rather than a fixed relational schema.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › NoSQL & Data Model
Definition
NoSQL in DynamoDB means items and attributes rather than fixed rows and columns. Items in the same table can have different attributes, enabling flexible document and key-value patterns suitable for rapid change and variable payloads.
Analogy
Think of a library catalog where some entries include publisher and translator while others include edition notes. The catalog stores items with differing fields but supports lookups by key.
Concrete example
UserProfile items: {UserID, Email, Username, FullName, Age}. Some items add deviceTokens or preferences when available. This flexibility reduces migration friction and supports varied client needs.
Key explanation
  • DynamoDB supports key-value and document styles; choose attributes to support queries.
  • Avoid thinking 'no schema' means no design — plan access patterns and keys first.
  • Use nested attributes only when your queries can reference them efficiently or when you don't need secondary indexing on them.
Common mistake
Assuming schema-less equals no planning — can cause inefficient queries later or need for costly data reshapes.
Key Takeaway

Design items around how your application queries data; flexibility is a tool, not a substitute for access-pattern planning.

screens.title: Primary keys: partition and sort keys
screens.narratorSegment: The primary key is the fundamental handle you use to locate items in DynamoDB. There are two forms: a simple primary key with only a partition key, and a composite primary key that adds a sort key. The partition key determines the logical partition where data is stored and influences how items are distributed across storage nodes. A well-chosen partition key evenly spreads traffic; a poor choice creates hot partitions and throttling. The sort key enables multiple items to share the same partition key and supports efficient range queries such as retrieving all orders for a user ordered by timestamp or order ID. For example, in an Orders table you might use UserID as the partition key and OrderID or OrderTimestamp as the sort key to fetch a user's orders with a single query. A common misconception is to choose an obvious attribute, like a username, without considering its distribution or traffic skew. Also, do not assume sort keys replace the need for indexes when you need to query by a different attribute entirely. Plan your partition key for even distribution and your sort key for the intra-partition query patterns you expect. How would you design keys for a leaderboard that needs global top scores and per-region queries?

keyIdea.title: Primary key design matters
keyIdea.text: Partition key determines distribution; sort key enables multiple related items per partition and efficient range queries.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Primary Keys
Partition Key (HASH)
Determines logical partition. Choose a key that spreads reads and writes evenly across items to avoid hot partitions. Example: UserID is often a good partition key for user-specific data.
Sort Key (RANGE)
Optional second part of the primary key to support multiple items with the same partition key. Use it for range queries, sorting, and grouping, such as OrderID or timestamp to get a user's ordered history.
Example: Orders table
Partition: UserID. Sort: OrderID or OrderTimestamp. Query: get all orders for a user, optionally with begins_with or between on the sort key.
Common mistake
Using low-cardinality attributes (like 'country' or 'status') as partition keys, which concentrates traffic and causes throttling.
Key Takeaway

Select a high-cardinality partition key for even distribution and use a sort key for range queries within a partition.

screens.title: Secondary Indexes: GSI vs LSI
screens.narratorSegment: Secondary indexes let you query attributes other than the table's primary key. DynamoDB provides Global Secondary Indexes and Local Secondary Indexes with distinct behaviors. A GSI can have a different partition key and an optional sort key from the base table, and it is global because it spans all table partitions. Use GSIs when you need to query across the whole table by an alternate key, like finding profiles by username or leaderboards by score. GSIs are eventually consistent by default and incur additional capacity costs because they maintain their own read and write capacity. An LSI shares the same partition key as the base table but defines a different sort key, enabling alternate sort orders within a partition and offering strong consistency. LSIs are useful when your query needs different sorting for items with the same partition key. A common misconception is thinking LSIs can replace GSIs — LSIs are local and limited to items that share the partition; use GSIs for alternative global lookups. Example: to query all users by username across the table, create a UsernameIndex GSI. Decide index types by whether your query must be globally available or only within the same partition.

keyIdea.title: GSI vs LSI
keyIdea.text: GSI: alternate global key, different partition possible; LSI: alternate sort for same partition key, strongly consistent within partition.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › GSI vs LSI
Global Secondary Index (GSI)
Defines a different partition key and optional sort key. Spans all table partitions, enabling alternative global query patterns.
  • Use when you need to query by a different attribute across the table.
  • Typically eventually consistent; has its own capacity costs.
  • Example: UsernameIndex to find a profile by username.
Local Secondary Index (LSI)
Shares the table partition key but provides a different sort key. Operates within a partition and supports strongly consistent reads.
  • Use when you need alternative sorting for items with the same partition key.
  • Limited to 10 GB per partition key value at table create time—plan capacity accordingly.
  • Example: alternate sort of orders by status or timestamp within a given user.
Decision guide
If your query needs to find items by an attribute across the table, choose a GSI. If it needs a different sort order for items that already share a partition key, choose an LSI.
Gotcha

GSIs add cost and eventual consistency considerations. LSIs are local and strongly consistent but limited in capacity use and must be defined at table creation.

screens.title: Capacity modes: Provisioned vs On-Demand
screens.narratorSegment: DynamoDB offers two capacity modes: Provisioned and On-Demand. With Provisioned Capacity you set read capacity units and write capacity units ahead of time. One read capacity unit corresponds to one strongly consistent read per second for items up to four kilobytes, or two eventually consistent reads per second. One write capacity unit covers one write per second for items up to one kilobyte. Provisioned mode is cost-effective when your traffic patterns are predictable because you can reserve capacity and optimize costs. On-Demand Capacity charges per request and scales automatically to handle sudden bursts, making it a better fit for unpredictable or spiky workloads such as new features, testing phases, or IoT bursts. A common trap is using provisioned capacity without auto-scaling for variable traffic; this risks throttling or unnecessary over-provisioning. When deciding, map your expected reads and writes into RCUs and WCUs and compare predictable usage to per-request pricing. Example: an IoT stream with intermittent bursts typically benefits from On-Demand, whereas steady background processing might be cheaper with Provisioned capacity. Capacity modes: Provisioned vs On-Demand means provisioned for steady predictable load (rcus/wcus), on-demand for unpredictable or bursty traffic to avoid manual capacity management.. In practical terms, choosing throughput strategy for predictable or bursty workloads. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Capacity Modes
Provisioned Capacity
You specify RCUs and WCUs. Best for predictable, steady workloads where reserved capacity reduces cost.
  • 1 RCU = 1 strongly consistent read per second (items ≤ 4KB) or 2 eventually consistent reads.
  • 1 WCU = 1 write per second (items ≤ 1KB).
  • Use with auto-scaling when traffic varies moderately.
On-Demand Capacity
Pay per request; DynamoDB scales automatically to handle sudden spikes without pre-provisioning.
  • Ideal for unpredictable workloads or early-stage apps where traffic is unknown.
  • Simplifies operations by removing capacity planning steps.
Decision example
IoT devices with bursty telemetry: On-Demand. A steady analytics pipeline: Provisioned with calculated RCUs/WCUs.
Pitfall

Choosing Provisioned without estimating RCUs/WCUs can cause either throttling (under-provision) or wasted cost (over-provision).

screens.title: Read and Write Capacity Units (RCUs & WCUs)
screens.narratorSegment: RCUs and WCUs express the throughput capacity DynamoDB provides in Provisioned mode. An RCU represents one strongly consistent read per second for items up to four kilobytes, or two eventually consistent reads for the same size. A WCU represents one write per second for items up to one kilobyte. These units let you translate expected request rates and item sizes into provisioned capacity. For instance, if your application performs 50 strongly consistent reads per second for 2 KB items, you need 50 RCUs. If you perform 200 eventually consistent reads for 2 KB items, you would need 100 RCUs because two eventually consistent reads consume one RCU. Misunderstanding item size leads to underprovisioning: larger items consume more units or require more units per request. A practical example: a profile write containing a 900-byte payload consumes one WCU; a 2 KB read that is eventually consistent consumes one RCU for every two reads per second. Always calculate RCUs and WCUs from both traffic and item size before choosing Provisioned capacity, and monitor CloudWatch to validate assumptions. Read and Write Capacity Units (RCUs & WCUs) means rcus and wcus quantify read and write throughput; item size and consistency type determine how many units each operation consumes.. In practical terms, how throughput maps to reads and writes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › RCUs & WCUs
What is an RCU?
One strongly consistent read per second for items up to 4KB, or two eventually consistent reads per second for the same size.
What is a WCU?
One write per second for items up to 1KB. Larger items consume proportionally more WCUs.
Worked example
If you need 100 eventually consistent reads per second of 4KB items, 100 reads / 2 = 50 RCUs. If you need 20 writes per second of 1.5KB items, each write uses 2 WCUs, so 40 WCUs total.
Common misconception
Assuming one request equals one RCU or WCU without accounting for item size or consistency leads to capacity shortfalls.
Key Takeaway

Translate your real request rates and payload sizes into RCUs and WCUs before provisioning capacity, and validate with monitoring.

screens.title: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)
screens.narratorSegment: DynamoDB Accelerator, or DAX, is a fully managed, highly available in-memory cache for DynamoDB that delivers microsecond response times for read-heavy workloads. DAX is A P I-compatible with DynamoDB so many applications require minimal code changes to use it. DAX is appropriate when your application repeatedly reads the same items and low latency matters, as in gaming leaderboards, real-time bidding, or rapidly updating dashboards. It handles caching logic and invalidation, reducing the read load on your base table and improving user-perceived performance. A common misconception is that DAX replaces good key design; it does not. If your partition keys are poorly chosen and create hot partitions, DAX can reduce table load but will not solve distribution problems entirely. Integrate DAX when read caching aligns with your access patterns and when you need to lower latency beyond what DynamoDB alone offers. Measure cache hit rates to ensure DAX yields the expected benefits and avoid paying for cache capacity you don't use. DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) means dax provides microsecond reads for repeated access to the same items, but it complements rather than replaces proper key and index design.. In practical terms, when to use an in-memory cache for microsecond reads. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › DAX
What is DAX?
A fully managed, in-memory cache that sits in front of DynamoDB and provides microsecond latency for repeated reads.
When to use
  • Read-heavy paths with repeated access to the same items.
  • Scenarios that require sub-millisecond response times for a large number of requests.
Note
DAX manages cache invalidation but does not replace the need for balanced partition keys; use DAX to complement good table design.
Concrete example
A gaming leaderboard that queries top scores frequently benefits from DAX because the same top entries are read many times and can be served from the in-memory cache with microsecond latency.
Key Takeaway

Add DAX for read-heavy caches where low-latency read performance justifies the additional managed cache layer.

screens.title: Avoiding hot partitions
screens.narratorSegment: Hot partitions occur when too much traffic targets a small set of partition key values, causing throttling and degraded performance. To avoid hot partitions, select a partition key with high cardinality and distribute requests evenly. Techniques include adding synthetic randomness to keys when appropriate, using composite patterns that include a high-cardinality attribute, or sharding logically related keys across prefixes. For example, if 'region' is low-cardinality and causes hotspots, combine it with a high-cardinality user ID or a hashed suffix to spread load. Another approach is to design access so that heavy-write operations are batched or routed differently. A common pitfall is applying randomness to keys that you still need to query deterministically; in that case, use a secondary index to expose a deterministic lookup path while the base table key is randomized for distribution. Monitor CloudWatch metrics such as consumed read and write capacity and throttled requests to detect hot partitions early. Example mitigation: for a write-heavy leaderboard, partition by leader group plus a shard number to spread writes across physical partitions. How would you detect and respond to a sudden hotspot in your production table?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Avoid Hot Partitions
Symptoms
High throttled requests, sudden spikes in consumed capacity concentrated on a few partition keys.
Mitigations
  • Choose high-cardinality partition keys.
  • Shard keys with suffixes or prefixes when necessary.
  • Use GSIs to provide alternative lookup paths if randomness prevents direct access.
Example
Leaderboard: instead of single partition for 'global', include a shard number: Global#shard-7 plus score sort key. Query across shards when building top lists, or maintain a GSI tailored to global queries.
Monitoring
Use CloudWatch to detect throttling and uneven consumed capacity. Respond by adjusting keys, adding shards, or switching capacity modes.
Key Takeaway

Prevent hotspots with high-cardinality keys or sharding, and validate with CloudWatch metrics to catch skew early.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Create Table (CLI)
Command (create-table)
aws dynamodb create-table \
  --table-name UserProfile \
  --attribute-definitions \
    AttributeName=UserID,AttributeType=S \
    AttributeName=Email,AttributeType=S \
    AttributeName=Username,AttributeType=S \
  --key-schema \
    AttributeName=UserID,KeyType=HASH \
    AttributeName=Email,KeyType=RANGE \
  --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST \
  --global-secondary-indexes \
    "[{\"IndexName\": \"UsernameIndex\", \
      \"KeySchema\": [{\"AttributeName\": \"Username\", \"KeyType\": \"HASH\"}], \
      \"Projection\": {\"ProjectionType\": \"ALL\"}}]"
Tip
If the CLI returns an error creating the GSI inline, create the table first and run update-table to add the GSI.
Alternative: update-table to add GSI
aws dynamodb update-table \
  --table-name UserProfile \
  --attribute-definitions AttributeName=Username,AttributeType=S \
  --global-secondary-index-updates \
    "[{\"Create\": {\"IndexName\": \"UsernameIndex\", \
      \"KeySchema\": [{\"AttributeName\": \"Username\", \"KeyType\": \"HASH\"}], \
      \"Projection\": {\"ProjectionType\": \"ALL\"}, \
      \"ProvisionedThroughput\": {\"ReadCapacityUnits\": 5, \"WriteCapacityUnits\": 5}}}]"
Key Takeaway

Map each CLI parameter to the conceptual model: attributes, key schema, billing mode, and indexes. Verify table status before populating items.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Put & Query
Put items
aws dynamodb put-item \ 
  --table-name UserProfile \ 
  --item '{ 
    "UserID": {"S": "user123"}, 
    "Email": {"S": "alice@example.com"}, 
    "Username": {"S": "alice_smith"}, 
    "FullName": {"S": "Alice Smith"}, 
    "Age": {"N": "30"} 
  }'

aws dynamodb put-item \ 
  --table-name UserProfile \ 
  --item '{ 
    "UserID": {"S": "user456"}, 
    "Email": {"S": "bob@example.com"}, 
    "Username": {"S": "bob_jones"}, 
    "FullName": {"S": "Bob Jones"}, 
    "Age": {"N": "25"} 
  }'
Query by primary key
aws dynamodb query \
  --table-name UserProfile \
  --key-condition-expression "UserID = :uid AND begins_with(Email, :prefix)" \
  --expression-attribute-values '{":uid": {"S": "user123"}, ":prefix": {"S": "alice"}}'
This returns items for user123 with emails starting with 'alice'.
Query using GSI (UsernameIndex)
aws dynamodb query \
  --table-name UserProfile \
  --index-name UsernameIndex \
  --key-condition-expression "Username = :uname" \
  --expression-attribute-values '{":uname": {"S": "alice_smith"}}'
Use this to find a profile by username across the table when username is not the base partition key.
Key Takeaway

Verify attribute type alignment and index projections; monitor consumed capacity and adjust design if you see skews or throttling.

screens.title: Common use cases and best practices
screens.narratorSegment: DynamoDB is a natural fit for use cases that require predictable low-latency at large scale: mobile backends, gaming leaderboards, ad tech, and IoT. The best practices that surface across these domains are consistent. First, design for access patterns: model your keys and indexes around the queries you will run. Second, choose capacity mode aligned with workload predictability — On-Demand for bursty IoT, Provisioned for steady, high-volume traffic. Third, add DAX when read latency must drop to microseconds and access patterns show repeated reads of the same items. Fourth, instrument and monitor: CloudWatch metrics for consumed capacity, throttles, and latency reveal hot partitions and misconfigurations early. Fifth, understand cost trade-offs: GSIs increase cost and storage, and DAX adds cache cost; evaluate whether index or cache better serves the pattern. Example: a gaming leaderboard may use a GSI for global top queries and DAX for frequent reads of top entries. A common misconception is treating DynamoDB as a drop-in S Q L replacement; instead, design to fit DynamoDB's strengths. How will you apply these practices in your next architecture review? Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Use Cases & Best Practices
Common use cases
  • Mobile backends needing low latency and flexible item shapes.
  • Gaming leaderboards requiring fast updates and reads at scale.
  • IoT telemetry ingestion with bursty traffic patterns.
Operational best practices
  • Design around queries first, then secondary indexes.
  • Pick capacity mode based on predictability and cost profile.
  • Monitor CloudWatch for throttles and partition skew.
Cost trade-offs
GSIs and DAX add cost but solve different problems: GSIs enable alternate query patterns, DAX reduces read latency and table load. Evaluate ROI before adding them.
Key Takeaway

Tune designs to access patterns, use indexes and cache where appropriate, and instrument to detect issues early.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essential concepts to carry forward. First, DynamoDB is a schema-less NoSQL service supporting key-value and document models; design is driven by access patterns rather than table schemas. Second, the primary key — partition and optional sort key — determines data distribution and supports range queries; choose high-cardinality partition keys to avoid hotspots. Third, use Global Secondary Indexes to query by alternate keys across the entire table and Local Secondary Indexes to provide alternate sort orders within the same partition. Fourth, capacity modes matter: Provisioned uses RCUs and WCUs and is efficient for predictable load, while On-Demand scales per request and is ideal for unpredictable bursty traffic. Finally, DAX offers an in-memory cache for microsecond reads in read-heavy applications. Keep monitoring and match your design to real query patterns. These are the decisions you'll revisit when designing or reviewing a DynamoDB-backed system.

NoSQL Database
A flexible, non-tabular storage model; items can differ in attributes.
Partition & Sort Key
Partition key controls distribution; sort key enables multiple related items and range queries.
GSI vs LSI
GSI: alternate global keys; LSI: alternate sort within same partition.
RCUs & WCUs
Units that express throughput; item size and consistency type determine consumption.
Capacity Modes
Provisioned for predictable loads; On-Demand for unpredictable, bursty traffic.
DAX
In-memory cache for microsecond reads; best for read-heavy repeated access patterns.

Design around queries, choose keys for distribution, pick a capacity mode that fits traffic, and add indexes or DAX to serve access patterns efficiently.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.narratorSegment: Keep three compact reminders when designing with DynamoDB. First, model for queries up front: choose partition and sort keys to match the queries you will run. Third, add the right tool for the job: GSIs for alternate global queries, LSIs for alternate sorts within a partition, and DAX for read-heavy hotspots that need microsecond latency. fullNarratorScript:
Today you will take a focused deep dive into Amazon DynamoDB, a fully managed NoSQL service that supports key-value and document models. We will build intuition for primary key design using partition and sort keys, see how secondary indexes let you query data in different ways, and compare Provisioned and On-Demand capacity modes so you can choose cost-effective throughput for different workloads. You will also learn when to add DynamoDB Accelerator, or DAX, to achieve microsecond reads for read-heavy workloads. Throughout the lesson we use concrete examples — a Users table and an Orders table — that show how keys map to real application needs like retrieving all orders for a user. I will highlight common mistakes, such as hot partitions from poor partition key choice, and practical monitoring advice using CloudWatch. By the end you will be able to design a UserProfile table with the right primary key and a Global Secondary Index and run basic AWS CLI commands to create and query the table. Think about an application you know: which queries are most common, and which attributes would you expose through an index?

By the end of this chapter you will have four practical competencies. First, you will understand NoSQL fundamentals and the DynamoDB key-value and document model, so you can explain why items need not share the same attributes and how that flexibility supports rapid iteration. Second, you will design DynamoDB tables with appropriate primary keys — partition-only and composite partition-plus-sort — and add secondary indexes where queries require attributes beyond the primary key. Third, you will distinguish between Provisioned and On-Demand capacity modes and select the most cost-effective option based on traffic patterns, including how RCUs and WCUs translate to reads and writes per second. Fourth, you will explain when to introduce DynamoDB Accelerator, DAX, for read-heavy workloads and what benefits it brings for microsecond response times. Each objective includes a short mnemonic or example so you can link the skill to a real scenario, like choosing on-demand for an IoT bursty stream or adding a GSI for leaderboard queries.

This second objectives panel focuses on hands-on skills and validation. You will practice creating a UserProfile table with a composite primary key and a Global Secondary Index using the AWS CLI. You will insert example items, run queries against both the primary key and the GSI, and interpret query output. The activity will teach you how CLI commands map to DynamoDB concepts, for example how the key-schema maps to partition and sort keys and how the billing mode argument toggles on-demand versus provisioned capacity. Finally, you will learn assessment heuristics: identify a hot partition by observing throttling metrics, and choose between on-demand and provisioned modes based on traffic predictability. These tasks give you evidence of competency: a working table, successful queries, and the ability to justify your design choices based on observed behavior.

NoSQL databases use models other than fixed relational tables to store data. In DynamoDB you work with items and attributes rather than rows and columns; items in the same table can have different attributes. This schema-less flexibility is powerful when your application evolves quickly or when different entities share storage but need different fields. Concretely, a UserProfile table might contain items with fields like UserID, Email, Username, FullName and Age for some users, while others might include device tokens or preferences. DynamoDB supports both a simple key-value pattern and a richer document style where attributes can be nested. The core trade-off is flexibility versus relational guarantees: you gain agility and scale but accept that joins and complex multi-row transactions are not the primary pattern. A common misconception is that schema-less means you do not plan the shape of your data; in fact, you should design access patterns and keys up front to ensure efficient queries and even distribution. Example: a mobile backend storing profiles and optional settings benefits from adding only attributes you need per user. Takeaway: think in terms of access patterns and item-level attributes before choosing keys and indexes. What common queries will your application run against the data?

The primary key is the fundamental handle you use to locate items in DynamoDB. There are two forms: a simple primary key with only a partition key, and a composite primary key that adds a sort key. The partition key determines the logical partition where data is stored and influences how items are distributed across storage nodes. A well-chosen partition key evenly spreads traffic; a poor choice creates hot partitions and throttling. The sort key enables multiple items to share the same partition key and supports efficient range queries such as retrieving all orders for a user ordered by timestamp or order ID. For example, in an Orders table you might use UserID as the partition key and OrderID or OrderTimestamp as the sort key to fetch a user's orders with a single query. A common misconception is to choose an obvious attribute, like a username, without considering its distribution or traffic skew. Also, do not assume sort keys replace the need for indexes when you need to query by a different attribute entirely. Plan your partition key for even distribution and your sort key for the intra-partition query patterns you expect. How would you design keys for a leaderboard that needs global top scores and per-region queries?

Secondary indexes let you query attributes other than the table's primary key. DynamoDB provides Global Secondary Indexes and Local Secondary Indexes with distinct behaviors. A GSI can have a different partition key and an optional sort key from the base table, and it is global because it spans all table partitions. Use GSIs when you need to query across the whole table by an alternate key, like finding profiles by username or leaderboards by score. GSIs are eventually consistent by default and incur additional capacity costs because they maintain their own read and write capacity. An LSI shares the same partition key as the base table but defines a different sort key, enabling alternate sort orders within a partition and offering strong consistency. LSIs are useful when your query needs different sorting for items with the same partition key. A common misconception is thinking LSIs can replace GSIs — LSIs are local and limited to items that share the partition; use GSIs for alternative global lookups. Example: to query all users by username across the table, create a UsernameIndex GSI. Decide index types by whether your query must be globally available or only within the same partition.

DynamoDB offers two capacity modes: Provisioned and On-Demand. With Provisioned Capacity you set read capacity units and write capacity units ahead of time. One read capacity unit corresponds to one strongly consistent read per second for items up to four kilobytes, or two eventually consistent reads per second. One write capacity unit covers one write per second for items up to one kilobyte. Provisioned mode is cost-effective when your traffic patterns are predictable because you can reserve capacity and optimize costs. On-Demand Capacity charges per request and scales automatically to handle sudden bursts, making it a better fit for unpredictable or spiky workloads such as new features, testing phases, or IoT bursts. A common trap is using provisioned capacity without auto-scaling for variable traffic; this risks throttling or unnecessary over-provisioning. When deciding, map your expected reads and writes into RCUs and WCUs and compare predictable usage to per-request pricing. Example: an IoT stream with intermittent bursts typically benefits from On-Demand, whereas steady background processing might be cheaper with Provisioned capacity. Capacity modes: Provisioned vs On-Demand means provisioned for steady predictable load (rcus/wcus), on-demand for unpredictable or bursty traffic to avoid manual capacity management.. In practical terms, choosing throughput strategy for predictable or bursty workloads. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

RCUs and WCUs express the throughput capacity DynamoDB provides in Provisioned mode. An RCU represents one strongly consistent read per second for items up to four kilobytes, or two eventually consistent reads for the same size. A WCU represents one write per second for items up to one kilobyte. These units let you translate expected request rates and item sizes into provisioned capacity. For instance, if your application performs 50 strongly consistent reads per second for 2 KB items, you need 50 RCUs. If you perform 200 eventually consistent reads for 2 KB items, you would need 100 RCUs because two eventually consistent reads consume one RCU. Misunderstanding item size leads to underprovisioning: larger items consume more units or require more units per request. A practical example: a profile write containing a 900-byte payload consumes one WCU; a 2 KB read that is eventually consistent consumes one RCU for every two reads per second. Always calculate RCUs and WCUs from both traffic and item size before choosing Provisioned capacity, and monitor CloudWatch to validate assumptions. Read and Write Capacity Units (RCUs & WCUs) means rcus and wcus quantify read and write throughput; item size and consistency type determine how many units each operation consumes.. In practical terms, how throughput maps to reads and writes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

DynamoDB Accelerator, or DAX, is a fully managed, highly available in-memory cache for DynamoDB that delivers microsecond response times for read-heavy workloads. DAX is A P I-compatible with DynamoDB so many applications require minimal code changes to use it. DAX is appropriate when your application repeatedly reads the same items and low latency matters, as in gaming leaderboards, real-time bidding, or rapidly updating dashboards. It handles caching logic and invalidation, reducing the read load on your base table and improving user-perceived performance. A common misconception is that DAX replaces good key design; it does not. If your partition keys are poorly chosen and create hot partitions, DAX can reduce table load but will not solve distribution problems entirely. Integrate DAX when read caching aligns with your access patterns and when you need to lower latency beyond what DynamoDB alone offers. Measure cache hit rates to ensure DAX yields the expected benefits and avoid paying for cache capacity you don't use. Hot partitions occur when too much traffic targets a small set of partition key values, causing throttling and degraded performance. To avoid hot partitions, select a partition key with high cardinality and distribute requests evenly. Techniques include adding synthetic randomness to keys when appropriate, using composite patterns that include a high-cardinality attribute, or sharding logically related keys across prefixes. For example, if 'region' is low-cardinality and causes hotspots, combine it with a high-cardinality user ID or a hashed suffix to spread load. Another approach is to design access so that heavy-write operations are batched or routed differently. A common pitfall is applying randomness to keys that you still need to query deterministically; in that case, use a secondary index to expose a deterministic lookup path while the base table key is randomized for distribution. Monitor CloudWatch metrics such as consumed read and write capacity and throttled requests to detect hot partitions early. Example mitigation: for a write-heavy leaderboard, partition by leader group plus a shard number to spread writes across physical partitions. DynamoDB is a natural fit for use cases that require predictable low-latency at large scale: mobile backends, gaming leaderboards, ad tech, and IoT. The best practices that surface across these domains are consistent. First, design for access patterns: model your keys and indexes around the queries you will run. Second, choose capacity mode aligned with workload predictability — On-Demand for bursty IoT, Provisioned for steady, high-volume traffic. Third, add DAX when read latency must drop to microseconds and access patterns show repeated reads of the same items. Fourth, instrument and monitor: CloudWatch metrics for consumed capacity, throttles, and latency reveal hot partitions and misconfigurations early. Fifth, understand cost trade-offs: GSIs increase cost and storage, and DAX adds cache cost; evaluate whether index or cache better serves the pattern. Example: a gaming leaderboard may use a GSI for global top queries and DAX for frequent reads of top entries. Let's summarize the essential concepts to carry forward. First, DynamoDB is a schema-less NoSQL service supporting key-value and document models; design is driven by access patterns rather than table schemas. Second, the primary key — partition and optional sort key — determines data distribution and supports range queries; choose high-cardinality partition keys to avoid hotspots. Third, use Global Secondary Indexes to query by alternate keys across the entire table and Local Secondary Indexes to provide alternate sort orders within the same partition. Fourth, capacity modes matter: Provisioned uses RCUs and WCUs and is efficient for predictable load, while On-Demand scales per request and is ideal for unpredictable bursty traffic. Finally, DAX offers an in-memory cache for microsecond reads in read-heavy applications. Keep monitoring and match your design to real query patterns. These are the decisions you'll revisit when designing or reviewing a DynamoDB-backed system.

Keep three compact reminders when designing with DynamoDB. First, model for queries up front: choose partition and sort keys to match the queries you will run. Second, pick the right capacity mode and translate real request patterns into RCUs and WCUs when using Provisioned Capacity; use On-Demand for bursty, unpredictable traffic. Third, add the right tool for the job: GSIs for alternate global queries, LSIs for alternate sorts within a partition, and DAX for read-heavy hotspots that need microsecond latency. These rules will help you avoid common mistakes like hot partitions or unnecessary indexes. When in doubt, instrument and iterate: build, measure CloudWatch metrics, and refine keys, indexes, or caching based on observed usage.
